facts.fact: In Spanish, the simple future adds an ending to the whole infinitive, so "hablar" (to speak) becomes "hablaré," meaning "I will speak."
facts.hook: a student writing to a pen pal keeps chopping "hablar" down to "habl-" and a friend spots the mistake

facts.fact: Regular Spanish verbs share the same future endings whether they end in -ar, -er or -ir, so "I will eat" is "comeré" and "I will live" is "viviré."
facts.hook: a kid memorizing three separate ending charts discovers they only needed one

facts.fact: Some Spanish verbs change their stem in the future tense: "tener" (to have) becomes "tendré," meaning "I will have," not "teneré."
facts.hook: a paragraph about next year's plans comes back with one verb circled in red

facts.fact: Spanish speakers often talk about plans with "ir a" plus an infinitive, as in "Voy a estudiar," meaning "I am going to study."
facts.hook: a grandparent answers a question about next year using a form the textbook chapter never mentioned

facts.fact: In French, the simple future is also built on the infinitive: "parler" (to speak) becomes "je parlerai," meaning "I will speak."
facts.hook: a student who learned Spanish first notices the French future works almost the same way

facts.fact: The French verb "être" (to be) has an irregular future stem, "ser-," so "I will be" is "je serai."
facts.hook: a sentence about being in grade eight next year needs a verb that looks nothing like its infinitive

facts.fact: French has a "near future" made with the verb "aller" plus an infinitive: "Je vais voyager" means "I am going to travel."
facts.hook: two friends argue over which future form sounds more natural in their summer-plans paragraph

facts.fact: English verbs have no future ending; English shows the future with helper words such as "will" or "going to" placed before the verb.
facts.hook: a language partner asks what the English future ending is, and the answer surprises everyone

facts.fact: German can form the future with "werden" plus an infinitive at the end of the sentence, as in "Ich werde Deutsch lernen," meaning "I will learn German."
facts.hook: a student keeps putting the main verb in the middle of the sentence and the German sounds wrong

facts.fact: German speakers often use the present tense with a time word for future plans: "Nächstes Jahr fahre ich nach Berlin" means "Next year I am going to Berlin."
facts.hook: a kid thinks a German friend made a mistake by using the present tense for next year

facts.fact: Mandarin Chinese verbs do not change form for tense; a future plan is shown with time words like "míngnián" (next year) or helper words like "huì" (will).
facts.hook: a learner searches a Mandarin grammar book for future endings that do not exist

facts.fact: Japanese has no separate future tense: one verb form, called the non-past, covers both present and future, and a time word like "rainen" (next year) shows when.
facts.hook: a student's sentence about next year seems to be in the present until the time word is added

facts.fact: Spanish nouns have grammatical gender, so a male dog is "el perro" and a female dog is "la perra."
facts.hook: a kid describing their female dog accidentally calls her by the male word

facts.fact: In Spanish, the masculine plural "hermanos" can mean brothers, or brothers and sisters together, so "Tengo dos hermanos" might describe one brother and one sister.
facts.hook: a classmate is confused when a girl with a sister and a brother says she has two "hermanos"

facts.fact: Spanish adjectives usually come after the noun they describe, so "a black cat" is "un gato negro."
facts.hook: a description of a pet sounds backwards until the word order is swapped

facts.fact: Spanish generally uses "ser" for lasting traits and "estar" for temporary states: "Mi hermano es alto" means he is tall, while "Mi hermano está cansado" means he is tired.
facts.hook: a sentence about a brother accidentally says he is permanently tired

facts.fact: French uses the verb "avoir" (to have) to give age: "J'ai douze ans" means "I am twelve," but word for word says "I have twelve years."
facts.hook: a student translates their age into French word for word from English and gets it wrong

facts.fact: French possessive words agree with the thing owned, not the owner, so "sa mère" can mean either "his mother" or "her mother."
facts.hook: a listener cannot tell whose mother is being described until they ask

facts.fact: The French word "animal" has an irregular plural, "animaux," and a pet is called "un animal de compagnie," literally "a companion animal."
facts.hook: a kid with three pets writes "animals" the English way in a French paragraph

facts.fact: In German, every noun begins with a capital letter, so "I have a dog and a cat" is written "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze."
facts.hook: a spell-checker flags every lowercase noun in a German description of a family

facts.fact: German has one word, "Geschwister," for brothers and sisters together, the way English uses "siblings."
facts.hook: a kid with three brothers and a sister looks for a shorter way to say it

facts.fact: Mandarin Chinese puts a measure word between a number and a noun: "one cat" is "yì zhī māo," where "zhī" is the measure word used for many animals.
facts.hook: a grandparent gently adds a missing little word to a grandchild's sentence about the cat

facts.fact: Mandarin has separate words for older and younger siblings: "gēge" means older brother and "dìdi" means younger brother.
facts.hook: a kid has to decide which word fits a twin brother born ten minutes later

facts.fact: Japanese uses different family words for your own family and someone else's: you call your own mother "haha" when talking to others, but a friend's mother is "okaasan."
facts.hook: a student politely describes their own mother with the word meant for someone else's

facts.fact: In Spanish, "¿Cuánto cuesta?" means "How much does it cost?" and is the usual way to ask the price of one item.
facts.hook: a kid at a festival food stall points at a dish and needs the price before ordering

facts.fact: To ask for the bill in a Spanish-speaking restaurant, a customer can say "La cuenta, por favor," meaning "The bill, please."
facts.hook: a family waits a long time for a bill that nobody asked for

facts.fact: Spanish speakers ordering politely often say "Quisiera...", a softer form of "querer" (to want) that means "I would like..."
facts.hook: a student notices the server smiling more when they switch from "quiero" to "quisiera"

facts.fact: In French, "Je voudrais..." means "I would like..." and sounds more polite than "Je veux...", which means "I want..."
facts.hook: a practice role-play where "I want" sounds rude and gets redone

facts.fact: French speakers ask a price with "C'est combien ?" or "Combien ça coûte ?", both meaning "How much is it?"
facts.hook: a kid at a crêpe stand needs to check if their money is enough

facts.fact: To ask for the bill in French, you say "L'addition, s'il vous plaît," meaning "The bill, please."
facts.hook: a student asks for "la note" or "la facture" and has to find the restaurant word instead

facts.fact: French speakers normally address a server with the formal "vous," not the familiar "tu," which is kept for friends, family and children.
facts.hook: a student realizes they just spoke to a waiter the way they speak to their little cousin

facts.fact: In German, a customer can ask for the bill by saying "Die Rechnung, bitte," meaning "The bill, please."
facts.hook: a class trip lunch runs late until someone remembers how to ask for the bill

facts.fact: In Mandarin Chinese, "Duōshǎo qián?" means "How much money?" and is the everyday way to ask a price.
facts.hook: a kid at a dumpling stall practices the question before reaching the front of the line

facts.fact: In Spanish, "para llevar" means "to take away," so a customer who wants food to go asks for it "para llevar."
facts.hook: an order meant to be eaten on the bus gets served on plates instead

facts.fact: In France and many other European countries, prices use a comma where English uses a decimal point, so twelve euros fifty is written "12,50 €."
facts.hook: a kid reading a menu thinks a sandwich costs over a thousand euros

facts.fact: In Japan, tipping in restaurants is generally not expected, and leaving extra money on the table can confuse the staff.
facts.hook: a server runs after a family to return the change they left behind

facts.fact: A mediator is a neutral third person who helps two sides reach their own agreement; unlike a judge, a mediator does not decide who is right.
facts.hook: two friends each expect the kid in the middle to announce a winner

facts.fact: An arbitrator differs from a mediator: both sides agree ahead of time to accept the arbitrator's decision, while a mediator only helps them find a solution themselves.
facts.hook: a friend asks to just be told who is right, and the mediator explains why that is not their job

facts.fact: The word "mediate" comes from the Latin "medius," meaning "middle," because a mediator stands between the two sides.
facts.hook: a kid literally sits between two arguing friends at a party table

facts.fact: Mediators usually start by setting ground rules, such as one person speaks at a time and no name-calling, which both sides agree to before talking.
facts.hook: an argument restarts twice until someone suggests rules for the conversation itself

facts.fact: In mediation, each person usually gets to tell their side without being interrupted while the other person listens.
facts.hook: a friend keeps cutting in until the mediator asks them to wait their turn

facts.fact: Paraphrasing, or restating what someone said in your own words, shows them they were heard and lets them correct any misunderstanding.
facts.hook: a friend realizes the fight started over something that was never actually said

facts.fact: A "position" is what someone demands, while an "interest" is the reason they want it; people with clashing positions often have interests that could both be met.
facts.hook: two friends both demand the same seat, but for completely different reasons

facts.fact: An "I-statement," such as "I feel left out when plans change," describes the speaker's own feelings instead of blaming, which makes the listener less likely to get defensive.
facts.hook: "You always ditch me" starts a fight, and a different sentence ends it

facts.fact: Reframing means restating an insult in neutral words, turning "She's so selfish" into "You want a fairer share," so the conversation can keep moving.
facts.hook: a mediator catches an insult before it gets repeated to the other friend

facts.fact: Mediators sometimes meet with each side privately, and this separate meeting is called a caucus.
facts.hook: a kid takes each friend aside one at a time at a family dinner

facts.fact: Many schools run peer mediation programs, in which trained students help classmates settle conflicts, usually with an adult supervisor available.
facts.hook: a student who trained as a peer mediator uses the steps outside school for the first time

facts.fact: Mediation usually ends with both sides agreeing on specific actions they will each take, so each person knows exactly what they promised.
facts.hook: a vague "let's just be friends again" falls apart the next day

facts.fact: Robert's Rules of Order, a guide to running meetings fairly, was first published in 1876 by U.S. Army officer Henry Martyn Robert.
facts.hook: a club president finds a very old book on the shelf when meetings keep turning into shouting

facts.fact: Henry Martyn Robert wrote his rules of order after he was asked to lead a meeting at his church and it went badly because no one agreed on how meetings should work.
facts.hook: a first-time club leader's meeting goes badly, and they learn a famous rule book began the same way

facts.fact: "Agenda" is a Latin word meaning "things to be done," and a meeting agenda lists the topics in the order they will be discussed.
facts.hook: a club meeting spends forty minutes on snacks because nobody wrote down what else to discuss

facts.fact: In meeting procedure, a quorum is the minimum number of members who must be present for the group's decisions to count.
facts.hook: three members vote on the club budget before the rest arrive, and others object

facts.fact: A motion is a formal proposal for a group to do something; under Robert's Rules, most motions need another member to second them before discussion begins.
facts.hook: one member's idea gets debated for ages even though nobody else supported it

facts.fact: Minutes are the written record of a meeting, noting what was decided rather than every word said, and a secretary usually takes them.
facts.hook: two members remember last week's decision differently and nobody wrote it down

facts.fact: Under Robert's Rules, a majority vote means more than half of the votes cast.
facts.hook: a club vote comes out five to four with two members not voting, and someone asks if it passed

facts.fact: Under Robert's Rules, a tie vote means a motion fails, because it has not won more than half of the votes cast.
facts.hook: a club splits evenly on a field trip and has to work out what happens next

facts.fact: A round-robin, in which each person speaks in turn around the circle, gives quieter members a guaranteed chance to share their ideas.
facts.hook: the shyest club member finally gets heard and has the best idea of the meeting

facts.fact: A timekeeper watches how long each agenda item takes, so one topic does not use up the time planned for the others.
facts.hook: the club never reaches the last agenda item three meetings in a row

facts.fact: A "parking lot" is a list where a meeting leader writes down off-topic ideas so they can be discussed later instead of derailing the current item.
facts.hook: a member's great but unrelated idea keeps pulling the meeting off track

facts.fact: A meeting chair decides who speaks next and usually calls on someone who has not spoken yet before letting someone speak again.
facts.hook: the same two friends keep talking while others' hands stay raised

facts.fact: Stating the problem as a shared question, like "We disagree about whether the ball was out," keeps the talk on the rule instead of on who is to blame.
facts.hook: a backyard game stops over one call, and "you cheated" is making it worse

facts.fact: In "divide and choose," one person splits something into two parts and the other picks first, so the divider has a reason to make the parts equal.
facts.hook: two cousins fight over the last piece of cake at a birthday party

facts.fact: In rock-paper-scissors, each choice beats exactly one other choice and loses to exactly one, so no choice is better than the others.
facts.hook: a kid insists rock always wins, and a friend proves it cannot

facts.fact: A fair coin toss gives each side an equal chance, which is why sports such as American football and cricket use a coin toss to decide how a game starts.
facts.hook: two teams argue over who goes first until someone pulls out a coin

facts.fact: The official Monopoly rules say that if a player lands on an unowned property and chooses not to buy it, the bank auctions it to the players.
facts.hook: a family game stalls when one player refuses to buy, and someone checks the rule sheet

facts.fact: Collecting money on Free Parking in Monopoly is a common house rule, not one of the official rules, which is why players from different homes argue about it.
facts.hook: a friend lands on Free Parking and expects a pile of cash the host family never uses

facts.fact: In formal chess, the touch-move rule says a player who deliberately touches one of their own pieces must move it, if that piece has a legal move.
facts.hook: a grandparent insists a grandchild move the knight they just picked up and put back

facts.fact: The phrase "according to Hoyle" means following the rules exactly; it comes from Edmond Hoyle, whose 1742 book set down the rules of the card game whist.
facts.hook: a grandparent says a card game must be played "according to Hoyle" and a grandchild asks who Hoyle was

facts.fact: Agreeing on a rule before a game starts is fairer than deciding it mid-game, because nobody yet knows whether the rule will help or hurt them.
facts.hook: a player suggests a new rule right when it would win them the game

facts.fact: In tennis, a serve that touches the net and still lands in the correct box is called a "let" and is replayed, a rule for handling an unclear point without blaming anyone.
facts.hook: two friends playing a net game borrow an idea from tennis to end a dispute

facts.fact: A referee or umpire is a neutral official who applies the rules, and players agree before the game to accept their calls.
facts.hook: a pickup game keeps stopping until a player sitting out agrees to make the calls

facts.fact: Scrabble players often settle arguments about whether a word is allowed by agreeing, before the game, on one dictionary to check.
facts.hook: a word game at a grandparent's house stops over whether "qi" is a real word

facts.fact: A 2001 study that observed children on school playgrounds found that other children were present during 88 percent of bullying episodes.
facts.hook: a kid realizes they are almost never the only one who sees the teasing

facts.fact: A 2001 study of school playgrounds found that when a classmate stepped in to stop bullying, the bullying stopped in more than half of the cases.
facts.hook: a kid hesitates, unsure whether saying anything could actually help

facts.fact: Researchers usually define bullying as hurtful behavior that is repeated and involves an imbalance of power, unlike a one-time argument between equals.
facts.hook: a kid tries to decide whether what keeps happening to a classmate is just joking

facts.fact: The bystander effect is the finding that people are less likely to help when many others are watching, because each person assumes someone else will act.
facts.hook: a whole group watches a classmate being teased and nobody moves

facts.fact: Teasing often depends on an audience, so walking away with the targeted classmate, saying something like "Come on, let's go," can end it without a confrontation.
facts.hook: a kid at a party pulls a teased friend into another room to help with the snacks

facts.fact: Distracting, such as changing the subject or starting a new game, can interrupt teasing without challenging the teaser directly.
facts.hook: a kid suddenly announces that the cake is being cut just as the teasing starts

facts.fact: Answering an insult with another insult tends to escalate a situation, while a short, calm statement like "That's not funny, stop" gives nothing new to fight about.
facts.hook: a kid's clever comeback makes the teasing much worse, so they try again differently

facts.fact: Checking in privately afterward with a classmate who was teased, and telling them it was not okay, can help them feel less alone even if nobody stepped in at the time.
facts.hook: a kid who froze during the teasing finds the classmate later to talk

facts.fact: Telling a trusted adult is not tattling when the goal is to protect someone from harm rather than to get someone in trouble.
facts.hook: a kid worries about being called a snitch for reporting teasing that keeps happening

facts.fact: An "upstander" is someone who speaks up or acts to support a person being mistreated, instead of only watching as a bystander.
facts.hook: a class discussion leaves a kid wondering which word describes what they did at lunch

facts.fact: Laughing along with teasing, even just to fit in, signals approval to the person teasing and tends to encourage them to keep going.
facts.hook: a kid notices the teaser glancing at the laughing group after every joke

facts.fact: Saving screenshots of hurtful online messages gives a trusted adult a record to act on, since messages can be deleted later.
facts.hook: mean comments in a group chat disappear before a kid can show anyone

facts.fact: With three strides between hurdles, a hurdler takes off from the same foot every time, because an odd number of steps keeps the same leg leading.
facts.hook: a runner keeps arriving at each hurdle on the wrong foot and counts their steps

facts.fact: An even number of strides between hurdles, such as four, means the hurdler must switch lead legs at every hurdle.
facts.hook: a runner who adds one extra step finds their other leg trying to go over first

facts.fact: The lead leg is the leg that goes over the hurdle first, and the trail leg is the one that follows, folding out to the side to clear the bar.
facts.hook: a runner keeps clipping hurdles with a trailing knee and a coach names the problem

facts.fact: Hurdlers try to run over hurdles rather than jump them, staying low so they spend as little time in the air as possible.
facts.hook: a runner leaps high over each hurdle and falls far behind

facts.fact: A sprint hurdler leans the chest forward over the lead leg while clearing a hurdle, so the body keeps moving forward instead of rising up.
facts.hook: a runner sitting upright over each hurdle lands slowly and loses rhythm

facts.fact: Hurdlers take off farther from a hurdle than they land after it; taking off too close forces the lead knee up steeply and slows them down.
facts.hook: a runner crowding each hurdle keeps hitting it with their knee

facts.fact: The lead leg should drive over the hurdle knee first and then straighten, rather than swinging up stiff and straight, which lifts the body too high.
facts.hook: a runner's stiff-legged kick makes them float over the hurdle

facts.fact: While clearing a hurdle, the arm opposite the lead leg reaches forward to balance the twist of the body.
facts.hook: a runner's arms flail over each hurdle and their body twists off line

facts.fact: Runners learning a three-step rhythm often practice with hurdles set lower and closer together than race spacing, then move them apart as they get faster.
facts.hook: a runner who cannot reach the next hurdle in three steps asks to move the hurdles

facts.fact: Both sprint hurdle races, the men's 110 metres and the women's 100 metres, have ten hurdles.
facts.hook: a runner counting hurdles on the track checks if the row is race length

facts.fact: At the Olympics, the women's 100 metres hurdles replaced the 80 metres hurdles starting in 1972.
facts.hook: a runner finds an old race photo and wonders why the distance was different

facts.fact: The hurdles in the women's 100 metres hurdles are 83.8 centimetres (33 inches) high.
facts.hook: a runner measures practice hurdles against the height used in senior races

facts.fact: The point guard is usually the team's main ball handler and is called the "1" in basketball's numbered positions.
facts.hook: a new player is told to "play the one" and does not know what it means

facts.fact: A pick, also called a screen, is when an offensive player stands still in a defender's path so a teammate can get free.
facts.hook: a guard cannot shake a tight defender until a teammate steps into the way

facts.fact: A screener must be standing still when contact is made; moving into the defender is an offensive foul called a moving screen.
facts.hook: a teammate's screen gets whistled because they stepped into the defender

facts.fact: In a pick and roll, after setting the screen, the screener turns and moves toward the basket, ready for a pass from the ball handler.
facts.hook: a screener stands still after the pick and nobody is open for the pass

facts.fact: In a "pick and pop," the screener steps away from the basket to an open spot for a jump shot instead of rolling toward the hoop.
facts.hook: the defense keeps stopping the roll, so the point guard calls a different option

facts.fact: Defenders can answer a pick by switching, meaning the two defenders trade the players they are guarding.
facts.hook: a guard comes off the screen and finds a new defender waiting

facts.fact: When defenders switch on a pick and roll, it can create a mismatch, such as a tall player guarding a quick guard or a short player guarding a tall one.
facts.hook: a point guard spots the smallest defender now guarding the team's tallest player

facts.fact: If both defenders go after the ball handler on a pick and roll, the rolling screener is often left open for a pass.
facts.hook: a point guard trapped by two defenders finally looks for the teammate cutting to the basket

facts.fact: Point guards often call plays with a hand signal, a number or a code word, so teammates know the play while the defense does not.
facts.hook: the other team keeps guessing plays because the calls are shouted in plain words

facts.fact: An assist is credited to a player whose pass leads directly to a teammate's basket.
facts.hook: a point guard who scored no points learns they helped score the most

facts.fact: The NBA adopted a 24-second shot clock for its 1954-55 season, requiring a team to attempt a shot within 24 seconds of getting the ball.
facts.hook: a pickup team stalls with the ball until someone suggests a shot clock

facts.fact: Danny Biasone, owner of the Syracuse Nationals, persuaded the NBA to adopt the 24-second shot clock in 1954.
facts.hook: a player wonders who invented the clock that keeps rushing their plays

facts.fact: In front crawl, swimmers breathe out underwater through the mouth and nose, so they only need a quick breath in when the face turns to the side.
facts.hook: a swimmer tries to breathe out and in during one short turn and swallows water

facts.fact: Breathing every three strokes makes a swimmer breathe on alternate sides, because an odd number of arm strokes switches which arm is recovering.
facts.hook: a swimmer who only ever breathes on one side starts swimming crooked

facts.fact: Lifting the head forward to breathe makes the hips and legs sink, adding drag; turning the head to the side keeps the body flat.
facts.hook: a swimmer's legs drag lower every time they look up for air

facts.fact: During a side breath in front crawl, skilled swimmers keep one goggle lens in the water and turn only far enough for the mouth to clear the surface.
facts.hook: a swimmer turning their whole face to the sky loses speed at every breath

facts.fact: In front crawl, the body rolls from side to side with each stroke, and the breath is taken as part of that roll rather than by twisting the neck alone.
facts.hook: a swimmer's neck gets sore from craning to breathe while lying flat

facts.fact: A swimmer's head pushes a bow wave that leaves a dip in the water beside the face, letting the mouth reach air below the level of the flat surface.
facts.hook: a swimmer notices a small pocket of air right beside their face

facts.fact: The urge to breathe is triggered mainly by rising carbon dioxide in the blood, not by falling oxygen.
facts.hook: a swimmer who holds air in feels desperate for a breath halfway down the pool

facts.fact: The flutter kick in front crawl should come from the hips with fairly straight legs, since kicking mostly from the knees creates drag.
facts.hook: a swimmer kicks hard with bent knees and barely moves forward

facts.fact: For most swimmers, most of the forward push in front crawl comes from the arms, while the kick mainly keeps the legs high and the body balanced.
facts.hook: a swimmer tries to kick their way across the pool and tires quickly

facts.fact: Almost all swimmers choose front crawl in freestyle races because it is the fastest of the competitive swimming strokes.
facts.hook: a swimmer asks why every lane in the freestyle race uses the same stroke

facts.fact: Johnny Weissmuller became the first person to swim 100 metres freestyle in under a minute, with a time of 58.6 seconds in 1922.
facts.hook: a swimmer times their own 25 metres and compares it with a famous old record

facts.fact: An Olympic-size pool is 50 metres long, while short-course pools, common in community centres, are 25 metres long, so a 25-metre swim is one length.
facts.hook: a swimmer's goal of 25 metres turns out to be exactly one length of their pool
